summary:
Kogi is not one of the twelve Nigerian states that administer Shari'a criminal law, so the death-penalty Zina provisions applied in Kano and Katsina do not operate on its territory. A visitor's exposure in Kogi is set by the federal statutes, which carry a 14-year maximum.

The Same Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act, passed by the House of Representatives on 30 May 2013 and signed into law by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014, applies in full in Kogi. Entering a same-sex marriage or civil union carries 14 years' imprisonment. Registering, operating or participating in gay clubs, societies or organisations, or making a public show of a same-sex amorous relationship, carries 10 years.

The Criminal Code separately criminalises sex between men with up to 14 years' imprisonment and gross indecency with up to 3 years, and both provisions apply in Kogi.

In 2022 a coalition of Nigerian human rights organisations won a court ruling that Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the 2013 Act breached the Constitution and could not be enforced anywhere in the country, Kogi included. The effect is that LGBTQ+ organisations and individuals may exist and organise. No comparable ruling covers the conduct provisions or the marriage prohibition, which remain enforceable against a visitor in Kogi.

The Constitution contains no specific protection on grounds of sexual orientation, and there are no federal anti-discrimination protections for LGBTQ people. A visitor targeted in Kogi therefore has no statutory discrimination claim to rely on.

BBC News reported on 9 August 2024 that mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people take place across Nigeria, including in Kogi, and are especially frequent in northern states. The report supplies no count, no dates and no named location within Kogi for those arrests.
tangentialFactors:
The twelve Shari'a-administering northern states impose penalties harsher than those available in Kogi, with death penalties applied in Kano and Katsina for lesbianism. Kogi instead sits under the federal 14-year maximum, and that difference is what sets the ceiling on its territory.

The 2022 constitutional ruling applies nationwide rather than to a single state, so the unenforceability of the organisational and public-show sections reaches Kogi on the same terms as the rest of the country. The conduct and marriage provisions were not challenged on that occasion and continue in force.

The same August 2024 reporting places the frequency of mass arrests highest in the northern states while also recording arrests in Kogi; the sources do not classify Kogi within that northern grouping, so the comparison cannot be resolved here.
localsOnly:
LGBTQ+ residents of Kogi have no protection on grounds of sexual orientation written into the Constitution and no federal anti-discrimination statute to invoke against employers, landlords or service providers.

Since the 2022 ruling, LGBTQ+ organisations and individuals may exist and organise in Kogi, because Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the 2013 Act cannot be enforced anywhere in the country. Residents remain exposed under the conduct provisions and the marriage prohibition, which the ruling left intact, carrying 14 years and 10 years respectively.

Residents are also subject to arrest and detention: BBC News reported on 9 August 2024 that mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people occur across Nigeria including in Kogi, without giving figures or a period for the state.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources provide no Kogi-specific prosecution, conviction or sentencing figure under the 2013 Act or the Criminal Code, and no dated incident of violence against a transgender person in Kogi.

The claim that mass arrests occur in Kogi carries no count, no dates and no named location within the state, so the scale of enforcement in Kogi cannot be assessed from these sources.

Whether the 2022 ruling has been invoked or applied in Kogi's own courts is not sourced here. The same is true of how police in Kogi handle gender presentation, identity-document markers, and the placement of transgender detainees in custody.

No sourced information covers access to healthcare, toilet or housing facilities, or recognition of a partner in Kogi beyond the national framework.
